evidence: execute() fetches entities via BookRepository/MemberRepository/LoanRepository interfaces and saves them via this.books.save / this.loans.save, which is orchestration rather than persistence code
Eligibility check is delegated: this.policy.assertCanBorrow(member, activeLoans, now) (domain service)
State changes are delegated: book.checkOut() and Loan.open(...) (domain entities)
Time and ID generation go through the application ports Clock and IdGenerator
Result is mapped with toLoanDto(loan, now), which is application-layer DTO mapping
Borderline: const STANDARD_PERIOD = LoanPeriod.ofDays(21) sets the loan length in the use case; arguably belongs in the domain but is only a minor configuration choice
parsedVerdict.reasoning: BorrowBookUseCase.execute only does application-layer work. It loads aggregates through repository abstractions, checks that they exist (not-found errors), gets the time and IDs from injected ports, and hands the business decisions to the domain: LoanPolicy.assertCanBorrow handles eligibility, book.checkOut() changes the book's state, and Loan.open creates the loan. It then saves through repository interfaces and maps the result to a DTO. There is no SQL, ORM, HTTP, framework or serialization code, and the eligibility logic is not written inline. One borderline point: the constant STANDARD_PERIOD = LoanPeriod.ofDays(21) sets a business parameter (the default loan length) in the application layer. It would arguably fit better in LoanPolicy or the Loan entity. It is still a value object built by the domain and passed into a domain factory, not a rule the use case enforces itself, so it is not a clear case of a misplaced responsibility.
